title: British Columbia Detailed Soil Survey: coverage and scale boundary
text: The AAFC British Columbia Detailed Soil Survey provides georeferenced soil polygons with links to component, soil-name, and soil-layer tables for agricultural areas of the Lower Fraser Valley. The 2015 specification contains differing scale labels across its overview, series identification, and polygon-layer name, while the current 2026 Open Government Portal record describes the series at 1:100,000. Preserve that uncertainty and consult the specific current dataset metadata before quoting scale. A polygon intersection supplies mapped regional context; it does not establish a uniform field profile, current root-zone condition, nutrient supply, salinity diagnosis, or management rate.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Canadian Soil Information Service

title: British Columbia Detailed Soil Survey: linked-table interpretation
text: The British Columbia survey separates mapped polygons from associated component, soil-name, and soil-layer records. The polygon links a location to a map unit, the component table identifies soils associated with that map unit, the soil-name table contains general soil information, and the soil-layer table stores properties that vary vertically. Do not collapse those relationships into a claim that one mapped class was directly measured everywhere inside an uploaded field. Use the map to target representative field inspection and sampling.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Canadian Soil Information Service

title: Estimated historical crop yields by SLC: verified construction and provenance
text: AAFC's Estimated Historical Crop Yields in Canada by SLC product combines three cropand region-dependent sources at the Soil Landscapes of Canada level. Provincial yields for seven major crops are downscaled to SLC version 3.2 with an AAFC statistical model that adjusts provincial averages using EVI2 vegetation indices before spatial distribution. Alfalfa, improved-pasture, and unimproved-pasture yields come directly from the EPIC model at SLC level. Prairie insurance yields are linked to intersecting SLC polygons where available. The sources are harmonized at SLC level using weighted averages. A value's provenance therefore depends on its crop and region; it must not be described as one uniform measurement method.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Science and Technology Branch

title: Estimated historical crop yields by SLC: verified identifiers, unit, crops, and intended use
text: The AAFC product reports estimated historical crop yield in kilograms per hectare and keys records with attributes including ECODISTRIC, SL, PROVINCE, and YEAR. Its crop fields cover major grains, oilseeds, pulses, forage, potatoes, beans, and other crops, including barley, canola, oats, rye, soybean, sunflower, wheat classes, corn grain and silage, flax, chickpeas, lentils, mustard, dry peas, potatoes, alfalfa, and pasture. The specification says the product supports Statistics Canada's Census of Environment, national-scale modelling, agricultural-model calibration, and agri-environmental indicator reporting. It is maintained annually and delivered as a comma-delimited UTF-8 CSV. Any answer using a value should preserve the crop, year, province, SLC identifier, and kg/ha unit. The regional historical estimate is not measured field yield, yield potential, or a current-season forecast.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Science and Technology Branch

title: Estimated historical crop yields by SLC: verified quality and interpretation limits
text: The specification does not define measures for completeness, logical consistency, positional accuracy, temporal accuracy, or thematic consistency. The lineage also shows that much of the product is downscaled, modelled, linked, or harmonized rather than measured as one field-level series. Treat an SLC value as a regional historical estimate with cropand region-dependent provenance. It does not prove a field's harvested yield, attainable yield, or yield potential, and it is not a current-season forecast. State these limits whenever the value is used to interpret an uploaded or drawn field.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Science and Technology Branch

title: Estimated historical crop yields by SLC: field-decision boundary
text: Use the AAFC SLC yield product to establish historical regional context and to compare records that share a crop, year, unit, and compatible provenance. It is not prescriptive authority: do not convert the regional estimate directly into a field operation, input choice, revenue forecast, or claim about current field performance. A field decision still requires current local evidence such as actual harvested area and moisture basis, farm yield records, crop and variety, weather, soil, management history, and field observations. Where those inputs are absent, ask for them instead of presenting the SLC estimate as a recommendation.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Science and Technology Branch

title: Nova Scotia Detailed Soil Survey: Pictou County scope boundary
text: The current AAFC Open Government Portal record describes the Nova Scotia Detailed Soil Survey Version 1 as 1:50,000 mapped soil and landscape coverage for Pictou County, with polygons linked to component, soil-name, and soil-layer tables. The broader overview language in the 2015 specification must not be used to imply complete province-wide detailed coverage. Outside the mapped product extent, disclose that no detailed-survey intersection is available. Inside it, treat the map as regional context rather than a current field soil test or a direct lime, drainage, nutrient, or irrigation prescription.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Canadian Soil Information Service

title: Nova Scotia Detailed Soil Survey: linked-table interpretation
text: The Nova Scotia detailed survey uses separate polygon, component, soil-name, and soil-layer structures. A polygon links a location to associated soil records; components identify soils within a map unit; soil-name records provide general information; and layer records describe properties that vary with depth. An uploaded field can cross multiple polygons and each map unit can contain more than one soil component. Verify current field variability, rooting, drainage, and representative samples before changing management.
publisher: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Canadian Soil Information Service

title: Prince Edward Island Detailed Soil Survey: island-wide context and field boundary
text: The AAFC Prince Edward Island Detailed Soil Survey provides seamless island-wide soil-landscape polygons intended for 1:75,000 representation, with linked component, soil-name, and soil-layer tables. The product can identify mapped soil and landscape context for an uploaded field, including where a field crosses map units. It cannot by itself establish present nutrient supply, erosion severity, compaction, drainage, or a tillage or fertilizer rate. Use mapped differences to design representative observations and sampling, then combine those measurements with slope, crop history, weather, and current local guidance.

title: Prince Edward Island Detailed Soil Survey: linked-table interpretation
text: The Prince Edward Island survey separates polygon geometry from component, soil-name, and soil-layer information. The polygon provides the spatial map-unit link, components identify soils associated with that unit, the soil-name table stores general descriptions, and the soil-layer table stores properties that vary vertically. A field intersection is therefore a mapped hypothesis about soil distribution, not proof that one soil or layer profile is uniform across the field.

title: Quebec Agro-Pedological Atlas: Monteregian coverage and attributes
text: The AAFC Agro-Pedological Atlas of Quebec is a vector data product for the Monteregian region, not complete province-wide field coverage. Its specification lists mapped or derived attributes including pH, organic matter, phosphorus, potassium, cation exchange capacity, drainage, depth to bedrock, slope, erosion vulnerability, texture, water stress, and agricultural capability. These attributes can orient regional interpretation and identify what to verify in the field.

title: AAFC Soil Erosion Risk Indicator: what the 2021 map represents
text: The AAFC Soil Erosion Risk Indicator, or SoilERI, estimates the combined risk from wind, water, and tillage erosion on cultivated agricultural land. It sums modelled erosion rates for representative landforms within each Soil Landscapes of Canada polygon using climate, soil, topography, and farming-practice inputs. The 2021 layer is a census-year, regional model result in a series from 1981 through 2021; it is not a current observation of erosion in an individual field.

title: AAFC Soil Erosion Risk Indicator: class meaning and trend meaning
text: SoilERI reports modelled average annual soil-loss risk in five classes: Very Low is less than 6 tonnes per hectare per year, Low is 6 to 11, Moderate is 11 to 22, High is 22 to 33, and Very High is greater than 33. A map label such as Very Low describes the modelled 2021 class for the intersected regional polygon. A Decrease label compares modelled risk across the 1981-to-2021 series; it does not prove that erosion is absent now, that the whole field has the same risk, or that historical soil damage has been restored.

title: AAFC Soil Erosion Risk Indicator: field-use limitations
text: Use a SoilERI intersection as regional screening context, not field truth. The indicator represents simplified and representative landforms within a Soil Landscapes of Canada polygon, uses the slope segment with the greatest modelled loss, and does not reproduce every real slope, drainage way, road, shelterbelt, terrace, cover crop, or other field feature. It excludes gully erosion and some cross-slope tillage effects, and the combined value is a simple sum rather than a process-interaction model. Specific places can therefore have greater or different risk than the mapped class.

title: AAFC Soil Erosion Risk Indicator: evidence needed after a map intersection
text: Before using the regional class for a field decision, determine which process is actually active and collect current field evidence. Inspect residue and soil cover, exposed or drifting soil, runoff pathways and gullies, slope shape and length, depositional areas, tillage direction and intensity, and within-field variation; review the separate wind, water, and tillage indicators where available. Management options must fit the farming system, soil texture, climate, and landform. A regional class alone does not select a practice, establish urgency, quantify measured field loss, or replace local conservation planning.

title: New Brunswick Agricultural Soil Classes: dataset construction
text: The official GeoNB Agricultural Soil Classes service maps polygons classified for agricultural suitability in New Brunswick. The service states that the project was completed by provincial natural-resources and agriculture departments using criteria established by the University of Guelph. The published layer exposes integer CLI_CLASS values rendered as classes 1 through 5; water bodies were removed and polygons smaller than 100 square metres were eliminated. The data were created in April 2021.

title: New Brunswick Agricultural Soil Classes: interpretation boundary
text: Use a GeoNB soil-class intersection as regional suitability screening context only. The service metadata does not provide enough detail to infer the limiting factor, current drainage, current nutrient status, crop-specific fit, or an input rate from a class number alone. Do not invent class definitions or treat an absent polygon as proof of a field condition. Verify current service metadata, soil and landscape observations, drainage, slope, crop requirements, and representative testing before giving field-specific advice.

title: Newfoundland and Labrador climate monitoring metadata: current-use prohibition
text: Never use the 2007-2015 Newfoundland and Labrador climate dataset metadata as current weather, a forecast, a current anomaly, a spray or fertilizer application window, frost confirmation, or a field sensor reading. A current operational decision requires a live authoritative weather source near the field plus local observations. Historical station metadata can only help frame climate variability or identify variables and stations for a separate retrospective analysis.
